mdl_consolidation_status.label: RESOLVED as of August 18, 2026 -- the JPML has ruled
mdl_consolidation_status.detail: The Judicial Panel on Multidistrict Litigation issued its transfer order on August 18, 2026 (Document 117, MDL No. 3191), centralizing the turnout-gear-only actions in the DISTRICT OF MINNESOTA before Judge Jeffrey M. Bryan -- not Montana (which the moving party and most parties had agreed to prefer at oral argument) and not South Carolina (Judge Gergel's AFFF MDL 2873, which 3M and other defendants had pushed for). The consolidated litigation is now captioned 'In re: Non-AFFF Firefighter Turnout Gear Marketing, Sales Practices, and Products Liability Litigation.' The panel explicitly drew a legal line: MDL 2873 is reserved for claims alleging direct AFFF chemical exposure/harm; these actions allege only PFAS-in-gear harm with no AFFF-exposure claim, so they get their own, separate MDL. Any future action alleging both would still go to Judge Gergel's MDL 2873.
mdl_consolidation_status.implication: This resolves the previously-unresolved venue question. Going forward, a new municipality joining this wave most likely becomes a tag-along action filed into or transferred to MDL 3191 in D. Minnesota before Judge Bryan -- a known, now-settled procedural path, which plausibly makes it EASIER (not harder) for new plaintiffs to join quickly, since the forum and judge are now fixed rather than contested. Minnesota's own role as host district (3 of the original 5 actions were already pending there, and 3M is headquartered there) is itself worth watching: no Minnesota municipality is currently a confirmed plaintiff, despite the state hosting the entire MDL.
mdl_consolidation_status.evidence_tier: VERIFIED (the actual order directly opened and read)

related_but_distinct_settlement.label: 3M just settled the OTHER, much larger AFFF litigation track for $7.35 billion -- not this one
related_but_distinct_settlement.detail: On November 3-5, 2026, 3M announced a $7.35 billion settlement (paid over nine years, 2026-2034, present value ~$5.8 billion) resolving nearly all personal-injury claims in MDL No. 2873, 'In re: Aqueous Film-Forming Foams Products Liability Litigation' (D. South Carolina, Judge Gergel) -- covering an estimated 115,000+ claims from people alleging direct AFFF chemical exposure. This is VERIFIED across multiple independent sources (Law360, Reuters, several plaintiff-firm trackers) and is a major, very recent development in the broader PFAS litigation landscape. It is explicitly NOT the litigation this tracker follows: MDL 2873 covers direct AFFF-exposure claims, while MDL 3191 (this tracker's subject) covers only PFAS-in-gear claims with no AFFF-exposure allegation -- the exact distinction the JPML itself drew when it created MDL 3191 in August 2026.
related_but_distinct_settlement.implication: Two live, open questions this raises, neither resolved here: whether 3M, having now resolved its largest PFAS liability, will be more willing to settle MDL 3191 on favorable terms next, or will fight it harder having already paid out its biggest exposure elsewhere; and whether any individual claimant with both an AFFF-exposure claim and a gear-only claim could end up navigating both settlements separately. Do not conflate this settlement with MDL 3191's status -- it changes nothing about this tracker's own litigation directly, but it is exactly the kind of adjacent development a sophisticated reader would expect this tracker to know about.

prediction_model.label: A real, sourced prediction of which states are the most plausible next plaintiffs -- built from two verified public datasets, with its own limitations disclosed as plainly as its findings
prediction_model.methodology: Two real, state-level, directly-opened federal datasets are combined: (1) FAA Part 139 certificated airport counts per state, as of the FAA's own September 3, 2026 status list (AFFF firefighting foam was federally mandated at these airports for aircraft rescue and firefighting for decades, making airport count a genuine, countable exposure proxy -- not a guess); (2) whether a state has enacted its own PFAS/AFFF firefighting-foam restriction law (a real signal of state-level political attention to this exact issue, compiled from multiple law-firm PFAS-legislation trackers, REPORTED tier since no single current authoritative government list was found). States already confirmed as plaintiffs are excluded from the ranking (14 states: AL, CA, CT, IL, IN, MA, MT, NC, NH, NM, NY, OH, TN, WV) since the question is who's NEXT, not who's already in. Ranking logic: states with BOTH an enacted law AND a higher absolute airport count rank first; absolute airport count (not per-capita density) is used as the primary tiebreaker.
prediction_model.methodology_correction_found_during_anal: An initial version of this model ranked states by airports-per-million-population, which produced a misleading result: Alaska, Wyoming, and North Dakota topped the list purely because they have tiny populations relative to even a handful of airports, not because they represent real litigation risk -- these states have very few municipalities or fire departments in the first place. This per-capita approach was discarded in favor of ranking by absolute airport count within the legislation-flag tiers, which produces a far more defensible result. This correction is kept here deliberately, as a record of a real methodology mistake caught and fixed, not hidden.

This is narrower than Colorado's or Washington's laws, which restrict sale/manufacture outright -- Michigan's is a training-use-and-reporting rule, not a sale ban, and that distinction should not be glossed over.

prediction_ledger.label: A prospective, timestamped forecasting record -- not a one-time claim
prediction_ledger.methodology_note: Each time this dataset is rebuilt, we snapshot the current top-10 predicted-next states with that date. Over time, we check which of those specific states actually show up in litigation_actions, and report the result honestly, misses included. This is the forward-looking version of the historical_validation_check above, which only looked backward. A snapshot's states were, by construction, NOT already litigating on the date of that snapshot -- the model excludes already-litigating states -- so any later appearance in litigation_actions is a genuine resolved prediction, not a restatement of something already known.
prediction_ledger.resolution_rule: A snapshot state counts as a HIT if it later appears in litigation_actions. It counts as a MISS only once at least 18 months have passed since the snapshot date with no litigation. Before 18 months, it is PENDING -- not yet a hit or a miss.

historical_validation_check.label: Checked against history: does early PFAS regulatory attention actually precede litigation?
historical_validation_check.methodology_note: For each of the 9 states currently in this tracker's litigation_actions, we researched whether that state had enacted PFAS/AFFF firefighting-foam legislation (a ban, phase-out, or reporting requirement) before its litigation was filed, and by how long.
historical_validation_check.important_caveat: The legislation checked here is about PFAS in AFFF firefighting FOAM. The litigation this tracker follows is about PFAS in firefighter turnout GEAR (protective clothing) -- a related but legally and chemically distinct exposure source. The honest claim this check supports is 'states with early PFAS regulatory attention generally are the states where PFAS litigation later shows up' -- not a precise claim that foam bans specifically cause gear lawsuits. Framing it as a tight causal mechanism would overstate what was actually found.

international.label: Beyond the US: Canada, Australia, and Western Europe
international.methodology_note: This is a first pass at the international AFFF/PFAS landscape, researched to the same evidence-tier standard as the US data (VERIFIED = primary source directly opened and read; REPORTED = secondary source only; explicit NOT FOUND where nothing checks out, never papered over). litigation.label: North Bay class action, $105 million
litigation.detail: Filed by Mann Lawyers against the Attorney General of Canada and the City of North Bay, in nuisance and strict liability ($100M property value loss/remediation + $5M punitive). Class covers owners of properties with private wells within 3km of CFB 22 Wing North Bay / Jack Garland Airport since Jan 1, 2017. Alleges DND firefighter training with PFAS foam at the airport from the early 1970s to mid-1990s contaminated Lees Creek and Trout Lake, North Bay's drinking-water source. Filed late 2025; allegations untested in court as of this research.

countries.regulatory_note: PFOS-based AFFF has been federally prohibited in Canada since the end of 2013 (narrow exemptions remain for residual PFOS already in equipment) -- regulated nationally, not province-by-province like the US. On September 26, 2025, Environment and Climate Change Canada opened consultation on a broader PFAS risk-management approach that would ban manufacture/import/sale/use of firefighting foams with any remaining unregulated PFAS (e.g., C6 AFFF) and restrict training/testing to closed systems only. Draft regulations are reportedly expected Spring 2027, final Spring 2029, though ECCC's own page leaves the exact timeline TBD.

countries.airport_foam_mandate: Transport Canada's Standard 323 (Canadian Aviation Regulations, paragraph 323.08(1)(a)) is Canada's direct equivalent to the FAA's Part 139 AFFF mandate. A June 2019 exemption allows airports to transition to fluorine-free foam under conditions; Billy Bishop (Toronto City) airport has done so. A 2024 report indicates multiple Canadian airports have delayed the switch pending a definitive mandate, meaning PFAS foam use likely continues at many. No complete current list of which airports have switched was found.

Reuters (Oct 16, 2026) reports the case is active and contested, with 3M arguing a public-nuisance claim is unavailable; this specific Reuters detail was seen only as a search snippet, not opened directly. countries.no_gear_specific_litigation_found: partial -- one unconfirmed lead (Wreck Bay Aboriginal Community Council v Commonwealth of Australia [2023] FCA 660) was found but not independently opened; otherwise NOT FOUND, which likely reflects that Australia's PFAS problem has centered on base/foam contamination rather than turnout gear specifically, not an absence of searching.
countries.regulatory_note: A national intergovernmental 'PFAS Position Statement' phases out PFAS use, plus a federal ban on import/manufacture/export of three main PFAS chemicals effective July 1, 2025. State-level foam-specific rules are a real patchwork, not one uniform law: Queensland was the first state to phase out PFAS firefighting foam; NSW banned training/demonstration use from 2021 with further bans from 2022 (with exceptions for catastrophic fires); as of a 2025 industry summary, only South Australia and Queensland have 'practically banned' all PFAS foams outright.
countries.source_name: federation.gov.au; dcceew.gov.au; NSW EPA, all directly opened

eu_wide_restriction_proposal.label: The broad EU PFAS restriction -- filed, not yet enacted
eu_wide_restriction_proposal.detail: Netherlands, Germany, Denmark, Norway, and Sweden jointly filed a roughly 14,000-chemical PFAS restriction dossier with ECHA in January 2023; public consultation ran March 22-Sept 25, 2023. ECHA's Risk Assessment Committee adopted its final opinion March 2, 2026. The Socio-Economic Analysis Committee reached a draft opinion March 10, 2026 backing a broad restriction with targeted derogations; its 60-day consultation closed May 25, 2026, with a final opinion expected by end of 2026. After that, the European Commission would propose the restriction for a REACH Committee vote. As of this research, it is NOT yet enacted.
eu_wide_restriction_proposal.evidence_tier: VERIFIED (multiple independent sources including HSE/ECHA process documents)

afff_specific_track.label: A separate, faster-moving, already-partly-enacted track for firefighting foam specifically
afff_specific_track.detail: Firefighting foam is governed separately under the EU's POPs Regulation, not the broad restriction above. Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2025/1399 (July 14, 2025) extended the PFOA-in-foam transition; the hard deadline to stop using PFOA-containing foam was December 3, 2025, which has already passed. A broader PFAS-in-foam concentration limit (reported as 1 mg/L, not independently verified against the primary text) with phased deadlines to 2030-2035 for certain fixed systems is also part of this track.
afff_specific_track.evidence_tier: VERIFIED for the PFOA deadline having passed; the 1 mg/L figure specifically is REPORTED, not confirmed against primary text

belgium.label: Zwijndrecht (3M) -- AFFF-connected, real litigation
belgium.detail: 3M's Zwijndrecht plant produced firefighting foam until 2002 and PFOS from 1976-2002. Roughly 1,400 residents sued; trial opened in Antwerp Feb 24, 2026, seeking roughly EUR28 million; verdict not yet found in this research. A prior case already produced a court-ordered EUR2,000 provisional payment to one affected family. 3M separately paid roughly $300 million settling with Belgian officials (distinct from the resident suit), and also faces a criminal investigation over PFAS waste disposal.
belgium.evidence_tier: VERIFIED-adjacent (consistent reporting across sources; the live trial's outcome not yet available)

netherlands.label: Dordrecht (Chemours) -- industrial manufacturing contamination, explicitly NOT firefighting-foam-related
netherlands.detail: Chemours/DuPont's Dordrecht plant (operating since 1962) is an industrial PFOA/GenX manufacturing-emissions case, unrelated to AFFF or firefighting foam. A September 2023 court ruling held Chemours liable for illegal PFOA emissions from 1984-1998; GenX emissions since 2012 were not found illegal due to insufficient evidence of harm at those levels. Separately, over 2,700 criminal charges have been filed against Chemours executives. No source found links this case to firefighting foam at all -- this is flagged specifically so it is never conflated with the Belgium case or with this tracker's main US AFFF/gear subject.

united_kingdom.label: Regulation confirmed; no litigation or contamination site found
united_kingdom.detail: The UK's Health and Safety Executive (acting as the UK REACH Agency post-Brexit) published its agency opinion on a PFAS-in-firefighting-foam restriction around June-July 2026, opening a 60-day consultation around July 21, 2026 -- scoped to foam only, explicitly not covering legacy contamination at sites like airports. The UK's own PFOA-foam transition deadline already passed July 4, 2025, on the same track as the EU. No UK litigation and no confirmed UK airport or military AFFF contamination site was found in this research pass -- stated as a gap, not a negative finding.
united_kingdom.evidence_tier: VERIFIED on the regulatory dates; NOT FOUND on litigation/contamination, explicitly not treated as evidence of absence

norway.label: A real, independently-enacted national ban -- the strongest Nordic finding
norway.detail: Norway banned PFOS in firefighting foam nationally in 2007. A separate PFOA ban in firefighting foam took effect July 5, 2025, per Miljodirektoratet's (Norway's Environment Agency) own published notice, implemented via produktforskriften (the Products Regulation) Sections 4-1/4-2, which also implements the POPs regulation; PFOS-foam export is separately banned. A broader EU REACH-style restriction (the EEA-relevant post-entry 82 restriction) is pending with multi-year transition periods, and it is not confirmed whether or when Norway's own implementation of that broader restriction takes effect. Confirmed PFAS contamination was found around multiple Norwegian airports, attributed to fire-training exercises -- a real contamination finding alongside the ban, not instead of it.
norway.evidence_tier: VERIFIED-adjacent (Miljodirektoratet's own page states the ban and the July 2025 date directly)

sweden.label: No foam-specific ban found; a real, large-scale remediation program instead
sweden.detail: No current Swedish law banning PFAS in firefighting foam was located, even searching natively in Swedish. A real, non-regulatory finding: Naturvardsverket (the Swedish EPA) together with MSB collected 416 tons of PFAS-containing foam from Swedish rescue services during 2022-2023 for destruction, and firefighting foam at training sites is explicitly stated to be Sweden's largest known PFAS source. A national ban on PFAS in some consumer products (clothing, shoes, cosmetics) from 2028 is proposed/under consultation, but is not foam-specific and not yet enacted.
sweden.evidence_tier: REPORTED (Naturvardsverket's own foam-collection program page); NOT FOUND for a foam-specific ban, stated plainly rather than implied

denmark.label: An early, real national ban -- 2006, ahead of most of this tracker's other findings
denmark.detail: Denmark banned PFOS-containing firefighting foam in 2006, with use of existing stock allowed until mid-2011. A later Miljoministeriet (Ministry of Environment) executive order bans import, sale, and use of PFAS-containing firefighting-foam concentrate specifically at training grounds, intended as a bridge measure ahead of the EU-wide ban; this order's current in-force status was not independently confirmed in this pass.
denmark.evidence_tier: REPORTED (government documents found via ft.dk/Retsinformation referencing the order; the consolidated current law text itself not independently opened)

finland.label: No national ban found; a real, confirmed contamination site
finland.detail: No Finnish national ban on PFAS firefighting foam was located, even searching natively in Finnish. A real, confirmed contamination finding: the Vantaanjoki river has Finland's highest recorded PFAS concentrations, attributed partly to an airport fire-training area. A 2026-effective ban on PFAS in consumer clothing, footwear, and impregnation products exists but does not cover firefighting foam.
finland.evidence_tier: REPORTED for the contamination finding; NOT FOUND for a foam-specific ban

european_firefighter_unions.label: NOT FOUND
european_firefighter_unions.detail: No statement from the European Firefighters Union Confederation (EFFUC) or any national European firefighters' union on gear-specific (as opposed to foam-related) PFAS exposure was found; all relevant hits in this research were US IAFF material. A dedicated follow-up search in German or Dutch was not attempted.

unverified_claims_flagged_not_used: A law-firm article's claim of '6,400+ PFAS legal actions globally' and a reported Swedish court ruling treating PFAS-in-blood as a legally cognizable injury -- both surfaced only via a search summary of a secondary article, never independently opened, and are NOT used anywhere in this tracker's claims as a result.

rest_of_world.label: Asia, South America, Africa, and the Middle East -- a first pass, mostly honest gaps
rest_of_world.methodology_note: Researched to the same evidence-tier standard as everything else in this tracker. Most of these regions have genuinely little to find on this exact question (PFAS/AFFF in firefighting foam or turnout gear specifically) -- that is reported plainly as NOT FOUND rather than stretched. A second research pass searched natively in Chinese, Arabic, Hebrew, and Portuguese/Spanish specifically for jurisdictions where the first English-only pass came back empty, since an English-only NOT FOUND is weaker evidence than a native-language NOT FOUND. That pass surfaced two new, real findings (China: a municipal-level Shanghai notice; Israel: a national draft policy) and confirmed several other gaps (UAE, Brazil's airport mandate, Uruguay, Paraguay) as genuinely absent rather than merely unsearched in English.

entries.label: A real but sub-national finding -- Shanghai only, not a national law
entries.detail: No national Chinese PFAS/AFFF firefighting-foam law was found, even searching natively in Mandarin. A genuine regional document exists: a joint notice from the Shanghai Ecology and Environment Bureau and Shanghai Fire Rescue Corps (沪环土「2022』200号 / Hu Huantu [2022] No. 200), citing the Stockholm Convention's 2019 move of firefighting foam from 'acceptable use' to 'specific exemption,' ordering Shanghai entities to stop procuring/selling PFOS-containing foam, with existing stock to be used up or disposed of within a set period. This is a municipal order, not national Chinese law -- do not generalize it to all of China.
entries.tier: REPORTED (the notice was located via Shanghai's own environment-bureau site, sthj.sh.gov.cn, which serves it as a direct PDF download; full text not confirmed independently opened in this pass)
entries.source_name: Shanghai Ecology and Environment Bureau / Shanghai Fire Rescue Corps, joint notice Hu Huantu [2022] No. 200

entries.label: A real, pending national policy -- not yet a finalized foam-specific ban
entries.detail: Israel's Ministry of Environmental Protection published a draft regulatory policy for PFAS in industry (June 2024) under the poisons-permit framework, estimated by news coverage to cover roughly 50-60 factories holding approximately 2,000 tons of PFAS-containing firefighting-foam concentrate. Coverage indicates the Health Ministry is pushing for urgent regulation while the Environment Ministry's position is less urgent; no finalized foam-specific ban was confirmed as of this research pass.
entries.tier: REPORTED (Calcalist news coverage and a Knesset committee document; the Ministry's own primary policy document not independently opened in this pass)
entries.source_name: Calcalist; Knesset committee documentation

entries.label: A real, enacted phase-out -- the strongest finding in this region
entries.detail: Singapore's National Environment Agency issued a circular (dated March 15, 2024) confirming that firefighting foams containing PFOA/PFOS, and later PFHxS under a Stockholm Convention listing, will be phased out of import and use effective January 1, 2026. Separately, Veolia was granted Singapore's first NEA license to treat PFAS-containing AFFF waste -- real treatment infrastructure built around this phase-out, not just a paper rule. No litigation found.
entries.tier: VERIFIED-adjacent (NEA's own circular directly identified; infrastructure claim cross-referenced via Veolia's own page)
entries.source_name: Singapore National Environment Agency circular; Veolia

entries.label: Confirmed contamination near US bases in Okinawa, no litigation found
entries.detail: Kadena Air Base and MCAS Futenma are suspected sources of PFAS contamination near Okinawa; the US military historically used AFFF there. In December 2025, USFJ (US Forces Japan) rejected Okinawa Prefecture's request for on-base access to test for PFAS; Okinawa Prefecture's own January 2026 report to the UN says it formally applied for an on-site survey. A March 2026 survey recorded new maximum PFAS levels near US airfields. Japan's government position is that it is 'difficult to say for certain' there is a causal link to US military activity. This is a real, ongoing contamination/access dispute, not a filed lawsuit -- no litigation was found despite how this story sometimes gets framed.
entries.tier: REPORTED (consistent reporting across sources; no litigation or primary government filing independently opened)
entries.source_name: pfascentral.org; Stars and Stripes; PFAS Project Lab

entries.label: Confirmed contamination near US bases, no litigation found
entries.detail: Routine testing at Osan Air Base (reported March 2026) found low PFAS levels. A March 2025 peer-reviewed study (Environmental Science & Technology Letters) found groundwater near US bases 'heavily contaminated' at potentially health-significant levels. South Korea's drinking-water standard is 70 ppt (PFOS/PFOA combined). A 2023 report said US command stated foams would be 'completely phased out' by 2024 -- whether that actually happened was not independently confirmed. No litigation found.
entries.tier: REPORTED (peer-reviewed study and multiple news sources cross-referenced; completion of the phase-out not independently verified)
entries.source_name: Stars and Stripes; Environmental Science & Technology Letters (peer-reviewed)

entries.label: A major, confirmed AFFF contamination event -- no litigation found
entries.detail: A fire at Ultracargo's fuel-storage terminal in the Port of Santos (April 2-10, 2015) was the largest fire in Sao Paulo state's history and involved large-scale AFFF use. Published volume estimates genuinely conflict across peer-reviewed studies: one (Water, Air & Soil Pollution, 2019) reports roughly 61,000 liters of AFFF drained into the environment; another (Miranda & Abessa, Marine Pollution Bulletin) reports over 460,000 liters of AFFF and PFAS-containing extinguishers used in the firefighting response. Both are real peer-reviewed papers describing confirmed PFAS contamination in the Santos estuary sediment. No lawsuit, civil action, or regulatory penalty tied to this specific incident was found.
entries.tier: VERIFIED for the contamination event itself (two independent peer-reviewed papers directly describe it); the exact volume is explicitly disputed between those two papers and should never be cited as a single settled number
entries.source_name: Water, Air & Soil Pollution (2019); Miranda & Abessa, Marine Pollution Bulletin

entries.label: Resolved (2026-11-08 pass): the PFOS-foam restriction is real and directly opened -- the "no PFAS regulation" claim was wrong
entries.detail: The original Resolucion 451/2019 Annex III PDF was directly fetched and read (argentina.gob.ar/normativa/332323_res451-3_pdf/archivo). Its PFOS section ("Acido perfluorooctano sulfonico, sus sales y fluoruro de perfluorooctano sulfonilo") contains, verbatim, a Class B firefighting-foam item with real operative restrictions implementing Argentina's Stockholm Convention PFOS exemption: (1) a ban on exporting or importing foam containing or liable to contain PFOS/salts/PFOSF, except for environmentally sound disposal; (2) a ban on using such foam for training; (3) a condition that testing use is permitted only where all releases are contained; (4) a requirement that by late 2022, use of such foam be restricted to sites where all releases can be contained; (5) a requirement for environmentally sound management of stocks and waste of such foam. This directly contradicts the earlier secondary source claiming Argentina has no PFAS-specific regulation at all -- that claim was simply wrong, or was describing a different, narrower question (e.g. no litigation, or no regulation on PFAS broadly beyond this foam-specific Stockholm Convention annex). Two things remain genuinely unresolved, not papered over: the PDF's readable text did not include the resolution's signing/effective date or its Article 5 (the document's creation metadata shows 2019-08-31, which is a record date, not necessarily the signing date); and a separate 2020 Boletin Oficial notice (detalleAviso 234441, published 2020-09-02) that reportedly replaced this Annex III with a new one ("IF-2020-51577401-APN-DNSYPQ#MAD") could not be opened -- boletinoficial.gob.ar refused the connection on two independent fetch attempts. Whether the 2020 amendment changed, narrowed, or left intact the provisions quoted above is NOT confirmed. No litigation tied to PFAS/AFFF was found in Argentina in this or any prior pass.
entries.tier: VERIFIED for the 2019 Annex III text itself (the primary PDF was directly fetched and its PFOS provisions read and quoted); the 2020 amendment and the exact signing date remain REPORTED/NOT FOUND
entries.source_name: Resolucion 451/2019, Anexo III (argentina.gob.ar), directly fetched and read

entries.label: Checked directly -- confirmed no current regulation or litigation
entries.detail: A Chilean law firm's own published analysis (Carey, titled 'PFAS: the litigation that is coming') states plainly that no current PFAS-specific regulation or litigation exists in Chile. Notably, even that forward-looking framing is anticipatory, not describing anything current. This is a real, checked, confirmed-absent finding, not an unresearched gap.
entries.tier: VERIFIED (a law firm's own published position, directly opened)
entries.source_name: Carey (Chilean law firm)

entries.label: A planning-stage roadmap, not yet an enacted ban
entries.detail: Colombia's Ministry of Environment, with GEF/UNDP support, is preparing a roadmap to replace PFOS/PFOA/PFHxS-containing foams (restricted internationally under the Stockholm Convention) with fluorine-free alternatives, focused on airports. This is explicitly in a diagnostic/planning phase -- no confirmed enacted domestic ban was found.
entries.tier: REPORTED-adjacent (a government planning document directly identified; not yet an enacted law)
entries.source_name: Colombia Ministry of Environment / GEF-UNDP roadmap documentation

entries.label: Acknowledged airport contamination at an international forum -- not domestic litigation or an enacted ban
entries.detail: Saudi Arabia presented a 2025 ICAO working paper to the Aerodrome Safety & Planning Implementation Group (Middle East region) describing PFAS-containing-foam contamination of soil and groundwater at airports and the practical challenges of phasing out legacy foam, citing ICAO Annex 14, the FAA's own transition plan, and EU REACH as references. This is a real, government-authored acknowledgment of the problem at an international regulatory forum -- not a domestic lawsuit or an enacted Saudi ban.
entries.tier: REPORTED (the working paper was found via search; the PDF itself was not independently opened in full)
entries.source_name: ICAO Aerodrome Safety & Planning Implementation Group working paper, Saudi Arabia

entries.label: Checked directly -- nothing foam-specific found
entries.detail: A September 2026 Engineering News piece covers an AECOM report calling for enforceable PFAS limits in South African water generally -- a proposal, not adopted regulation, and about water broadly, not firefighting foam specifically. A Werksmans legal update notes South Africa's POP Regulations now cover general PFAS waste-management duties, which is also not foam-specific. South Africa is reportedly one of 5 countries in the ICAO/UNEP 'FIRE' airport-foam-transition project (see Nigeria and Egypt entries below), but this was not independently confirmed for South Africa specifically in this pass -- flagged, not claimed.
entries.tier: REPORTED (both sources directly identified; neither is a foam-specific finding)
entries.source_name: Engineering News; Werksmans legal update

entries.label: A real international program, not a domestic Nigerian law
entries.detail: Nigeria's Civil Aviation Authority (NCAA) is hosting an ICAO/UNEP 'FIRE' (Fortifying Infrastructure for Responsible Extinguishment) project mission, assessing firefighting systems at Nnamdi Azikiwe International Airport (Abuja) and Port Harcourt International Airport for transition to fluorine-free (F3) foam. This is a program-wide effort, not Nigeria-specific: $82.5M total ($10M GEF-funded plus $72.5M co-financing), covering roughly 40 airports over 60 months across 5 African countries (Nigeria, Egypt, Ethiopia, Kenya, South Africa per UNEP's own press release), targeting removal of about 4,500 tonnes of PFAS-contaminated material and disposal of about 130 tonnes of PFAS foam concentrate. No separate Nigerian national ban or litigation was found.
entries.tier: REPORTED (NCAA's own social-media post and Nigerian news outlets are primary-adjacent; the UNEP/ICAO press release confirms the program itself)
entries.source_name: UNEP/ICAO FIRE project press release; NCAA; Nigerian news coverage

entries.label: Same international program as Nigeria -- not a separate Egyptian law
entries.detail: Egypt's Civil Aviation Authority is also part of the ICAO/UNEP FIRE project (see Nigeria entry for program-wide details), covering 3 Egyptian airports, with implementation planned 2025-2030; Cairo hosted the project's 3rd steering-committee meeting. No separate national Egyptian PFAS foam ban was found beyond this program.
entries.tier: REPORTED (Arabic-language Egyptian news sources identified; the program itself confirmed via UNEP/ICAO's own materials)
entries.source_name: UNEP/ICAO FIRE project; Egyptian news coverage

entries.label: No Italian national law yet -- a real, growing municipal campaign
entries.detail: No Italian national PFAS/AFFF firefighting-foam law exists; Italy is bound only by EU Regulation 2024/2462 (bans foam use for training/testing except with full containment) and EU-wide operator duties starting 23 October 2026. Italian sources explicitly confirm no Italian law exists yet. A campaign for a national ban, originating in the Veneto region (the site of Italy's well-known industrial PFAS water-contamination scandal, which is explicitly a separate, unrelated story from firefighting foam -- not conflated here), launched January 2026 with 129 municipalities in favor as of this research pass. A separate, unverified claim that 4 firefighters in Tuscany may have died from PFAS exposure was reported by one Italian outlet but not independently confirmed -- flagged, not treated as fact.
entries.tier: REPORTED (Italian news sources directly identified); the Tuscany deaths claim is explicitly unverified, not a confirmed finding
entries.source_name: L'Indipendente; Linkiesta; Il Fatto Quotidiano

entries.label: No Polish national law -- EU timeline only
entries.detail: No Polish national PFAS/AFFF firefighting-foam law was found; regulation is at the EU level only (Regulation (EU) 2025/1988). For portable extinguishers specifically, one commercial source (not the Official Journal) reports PFAS-foam sales banned from 23 October 2026 with use allowed until 31 December 2030, and alcohol-resistant foams carrying a later deadline of 23 April 2027 -- these specific dates are REPORTED only, not independently confirmed against the Official Journal text. No Polish implementing act was found.
entries.tier: REPORTED (EU regulation identified directly; specific extinguisher-type deadlines sourced from a commercial summary, not the primary legal text)
entries.source_name: Inforlex (commercial legal-text summary); EU Regulation 2025/1988

entries.label: No national ban found; a real, narrow maritime rule applies
entries.detail: No Russian federal PFAS/AFFF firefighting-foam ban was found, even searching natively in Russian; general POPs/PFOS restrictions exist via Customs Union (Russia/Belarus/Kazakhstan) treaty obligations, not foam-specific. A 2007 EMERCOM (Russia's emergency-response ministry) guidance document describes fluorinated-foam use with no phase-out language, and may now be outdated. One real, narrow finding: Russian maritime law bans PFOS-containing foam storage/use on ships built from 1 January 2026, under IMO SOLAS amendments -- an international shipping rule, not a domestic land-based ban.
entries.tier: NOT FOUND for a national land-based ban; REPORTED for the maritime/SOLAS-derived rule
entries.source_name: OECD Russia PFAS country sheet

entries.label: No national ban found; same narrow maritime rule as Russia
entries.detail: No Turkish-specific PFAS/AFFF firefighting-foam ban or regulation was found, even searching natively in Turkish. One Turkish news source confirms no comprehensive PFAS ban exists yet in Turkey, anticipating future pressure from EU harmonization (undated, currency unconfirmed). In the maritime sector, a Turk Loydu bulletin confirms the same SOLAS-derived PFOS-foam rule for ships built from 2026 applies to Turkish-flagged vessels -- again international, not domestic.
entries.tier: NOT FOUND for national regulation; REPORTED for the maritime/SOLAS-derived rule
entries.source_name: Turk Loydu bulletin

entries.label: No federal law; a real, confirmed contamination site
entries.detail: No Austrian federal PFAS/AFFF firefighting-foam law exists beyond EU rules. Provincial fire brigades (e.g. in Niederosterreich) have internally directed fire departments to stop using fluorinated foam, though this is administrative practice, not binding law. A real, confirmed contamination site exists at the OMV refinery in Schwechat, caused by fire-brigade foam use. No litigation was found.
entries.tier: REPORTED (Tiroler Tageszeitung directly identified the Schwechat site; no primary government document independently opened)
entries.source_name: Tiroler Tageszeitung

entries.label: No federal ban; real contamination signals and an agency evaluating action
entries.detail: No Swiss federal firefighting-foam ban was found. BAFU (the Federal Office for the Environment) identifies firefighting foam as a major PFAS groundwater source (training sites, industrial areas) and is evaluating an action plan; a reporting duty for PFOS-foam stocks already exists under ChemRRV Annex 1.16. Swiss media expects Switzerland will likely follow the EU ban once finalized, but nothing is enacted yet. Real, confirmed contamination signals: a drinking-water restriction near Basel airport, and a Valais cantonal authority flagging groundwater contamination from firefighting foam. No litigation was found.
entries.tier: REPORTED (BAFU's own stated position on foam as a PFAS source; Basel airport and Valais findings via Swiss media, not independently opened primary documents)
entries.source_name: BAFU (Swiss Federal Office for the Environment); Beobachter; SRF

entries.label: A real, dated national implementation of the EU PFOA restriction
entries.detail: Portugal's environmental agency (APA) confirms that as of December 3, 2025, no use of PFOA-containing firefighting foam is permitted -- the derogation period for already-installed stock ended on that date. This is Portugal's domestic application of the EU-wide PFOA restriction, not an independent national law, but it is a real, dated, primary-adjacent fact.
entries.tier: REPORTED (APA's own page identified; not independently confirmed as fully opened)
entries.source_name: APA (Agencia Portuguesa do Ambiente)

not_included: India: NOT FOUND, confirmed more strongly via a native-language (Hindi) pass. A 2025 academic review states India's Central Pollution Control Board has no PFAS-specific regulations and no national PFAS/PFOS/PTFE monitoring program; no firefighting-foam-specific rule found in either language.

UAE: NOT FOUND even after three separate Arabic-language search passes (general terms, standards-authority-specific, and airport/utility-specific). One vendor marketing page claims Dubai/Al Maktoum airports are 'subject to ICAO guidelines' moving toward fluorine-free foam, but this is uncorroborated by any GCAA or Dubai Airports primary source and is not citable.

Jordan and Lebanon: NOT FOUND via Arabic-language search. Only generic/global PFAS explainer pages and, for Lebanon, a vendor page confirming AFFF foam is still commercially sold with no PFAS-content regulation found.

Mexico: NOT FOUND via Spanish-language search. No DOF (official gazette), Semarnat, or Profepa regulation located; only commercial distributor blogs noting insurer and PEMEX-linked pressure to transition to fluorine-free foam.

Spain: NOT FOUND for a domestic ban or litigation via Spanish-language search -- Spain is bound only by the EU-wide REACH restriction already noted above; no Spanish court case or airport/base contamination suit located.

Brazil's airport-AFFF-mandate equivalent to the FAA's Part 139: NOT FOUND even after a native-language (Portuguese) search of ANAC, ANVISA, and CONAMA sources. A general PFAS bill (PL 2726/2023) is pending in Congress but not foam-specific or enacted.
Uruguay and Paraguay: NOT FOUND in either English or native-language (Spanish) passes.

Peru: still a thin, unconfirmed lead after a follow-up pass -- Peru's RETC emissions registry (DS 018-2021-MINAM) tracks PFOS/PFOS-F as monitored substances, but no specific decree implementing a firefighting-foam import ban was located despite checking El Peruano and MINAM directly.
Ecuador: NOT FOUND for foam specifically, confirmed again -- only general Stockholm Convention/PFAS context, no firefighting-foam-specific prohibition.

Vietnam, Thailand, Indonesia, Philippines, and Malaysia: all NOT FOUND or thin-unconfirmed via native-language (Vietnamese, Thai, Indonesian, Filipino, Malay) search passes -- all 5 are Stockholm Convention parties in principle, but none has a confirmed enacted national AFFF-foam ban, contamination event, or litigation action citable at this tier.
No African Union or Gulf Cooperation Group regional PFAS action was found (Mercosur not re-checked in this pass).

Ethiopia and Kenya: reported as part of the same 5-country ICAO/UNEP 'FIRE' airport-foam-transition program as Nigeria and Egypt (see those entries), but not independently verified for these two countries specifically in this pass.

DuPont.legal_name: EIDP, Inc. (formerly E. I. du Pont de Nemours and Company) -- named in litigation as "DuPont" or "EIDP Inc."

structure_note.label: The single most consequential corporate-structure fact in this entire tracker: liability was deliberately split across three companies in 2015 and 2019
structure_note.detail: The entity sued as "DuPont" today is almost never the same legal entity that made PFOA-era decisions. In 2015, DuPont spun off its performance-chemicals business as The Chemours Company, under a Separation Agreement (June 26, 2015) that defines how PFOA-related "Indemnifiable Losses" are shared between EID (the renamed legacy entity, now EIDP, Inc.) and Chemours. In 2019, DuPont itself split again into Dow, DuPont de Nemours, Inc., and Corteva, further separating the surviving brand name from the pre-2015 legacy entity. A binding January 2021 MOU between EIDP, Corteva, DuPont de Nemours, and Chemours now governs sharing of PFAS costs tied to pre-July-2015 conduct, capped at $4.0 billion in aggregate qualified spend or December 31, 2040, whichever comes first. Chemours has separately disputed indemnifying EID for claims alleging the 2015 spinoff itself was a fraudulent transfer -- meaning the companies are still actively litigating against each other over who pays, not just defending jointly against plaintiffs. For an underwriter: a judgment against "DuPont" in a turnout-gear case does not tell you which of these three balance sheets actually absorbs it without checking which entity was named and what the MOU's cost-sharing formula says for that period.

Honeywell.legal_name: Honeywell International Inc. (a Honeywell subsidiary is separately named as a turnout-gear seller in at least one action)

structure_note.label: A sharper open question (2026-11-08 update): the general allocation rule is now known, but the specific schedule that would resolve it is not public
structure_note.detail: The actual Separation and Distribution Agreement between Honeywell and Solstice Advanced Materials Inc. (SEC Exhibit 2.1 to Solstice's Form 10, filed 2025-08-21) was directly fetched and read in full (over 350,000 characters). It contains zero mentions of "PFAS," "turnout," or "firefighter" -- this is a general corporate-separation contract, not litigation-specific. Its general allocation rule (Section 1.1(173), the "SpinCo Liabilities" definition) is a catch-all: any Liability "to the extent relating to, arising out of or resulting from the SpinCo [Solstice] Business," REGARDLESS of when it arose, becomes Solstice's, unless it is specifically carved out and listed as a "Specified RemainCo Liability" on a schedule. The mirror-image rule in the "RemainCo Liabilities" definition works the same way for Honeywell. This means the turnout-gear liability most plausibly follows whichever entity made the fluorine-chemistry product actually alleged to be in the gear -- but the schedules that would name the specific pending Actions and carve-outs (Schedule 1.1(173)(x)(a), the "Specified RemainCo Liabilities" schedule, etc.) are NOT included in the publicly filed exhibit -- the agreement ends at the signature page with no schedules attached, which is standard SEC practice under Item 601(a)(5) of Regulation S-K (schedules may be omitted with an undertaking to furnish them to the SEC on request). So the general contractual mechanism is now understood and documented, but the specific answer for this lawsuit remains genuinely unavailable from public filings, not merely unresearched.

policy_exclusions.label: Object: Policy Exclusions -- how a litigation docket actually maps onto CGL policy language, not just who's named
policy_exclusions.methodology_note: This tracker already has two of the three objects a real insurance ontology needs: Object Defendant/Company (the corporate-structure layer) and Object Statute (the state presumption laws on the Presumption tracker). This is the third: the actual policy-wording question that determines whether a given PFAS claim is even covered at all -- the Commercial General Liability (CGL) pollution exclusion. This section is deliberately scoped to what is real and checkable, not a general insurance-coverage treatise.

drafting_history.label: The pollution exclusion's own history is itself a live legal argument in PFAS coverage disputes
drafting_history.detail: A limited "sudden and accidental" pollution exclusion first appeared as a 1970 CGL endorsement and was incorporated into ISO's standard form in 1973. The much broader "absolute" pollution exclusion removed that sudden-and-accidental carve-out and was incorporated into ISO's standard CGL form in 1986 -- a revision commentators note is not actually "absolute" in practice (a more accurate label used by some insurance-law commentators is "broad form pollution exclusion"). Policyholder-side commentary argues the insurance industry itself told regulators in the 1980s that the exclusion would not eliminate CGL's foundational products-liability coverage -- a drafting-history argument now being actively litigated in PFAS coverage disputes. Courts remain split: one secondary source claims roughly half of states have found the "absolute" pollution exclusion ambiguous in at least some contexts (not independently verified against primary case counts).
drafting_history.tier: REPORTED (secondary legal-industry commentary on policy drafting history, not independently opened at ISO's own archived filings)
drafting_history.source_name: IRMI; Hunton Andrews Kurth; insurance-industry legal commentary

real_cases.label: Fire-Dex's own insurer denied coverage for the turnout-gear firefighter suits -- a real coverage dispute involving a defendant already in this tracker's Company layer
real_cases.detail: In the underlying Fire-Dex matter, firefighters alleged PFAS exposure from turnout gear caused cancer. Fire-Dex's insurer, Admiral, denied coverage -- reportedly under both an "occupational disease exclusion" and (separately contested) a Total Pollution Exclusion. A federal court in the Northern District of Ohio held coverage was barred under the occupational-disease exclusion specifically, and noted there was insufficient Ohio case law to confidently predict how Ohio courts would resolve the pollution-exclusion question on its own. This is directly relevant to this tracker's own Company entry for Fire-Dex LLC: even if a plaintiff wins a judgment against Fire-Dex, whether Fire-Dex's own insurer pays depends on exactly this kind of exclusion-language dispute -- a real link between a named defendant already tracked here and the policy-wording question underneath it.
